concepts.name: Bonding types in solids
concepts.summary: Explain how metallic, ionic, covalent and secondary bonds arise and how bond type relates to general properties like conductivity and melting point.

concepts.name: Material classes and their traits
concepts.summary: Recall the four main material classes and the typical properties that distinguish each, such as ductility in metals, hardness and brittleness in ceramics, and low density in polymers.

concepts.name: Crystalline versus amorphous structure
concepts.summary: Distinguish ordered crystalline arrangements from amorphous ones and describe how this affects behaviour.

concepts.name: Unit cells and common lattices
concepts.summary: Identify the FCC, BCC and HCP unit cells and state their coordination and atomic packing.

concepts.name: Stress and strain definitions
concepts.summary: Define engineering stress and strain and explain why normalising force and length makes results comparable between specimens.

concepts.name: Elastic versus plastic deformation
concepts.summary: Explain the difference between recoverable and permanent deformation and relate it to atomic bonds stretching versus atoms slipping.

concepts.name: Basic property vocabulary
concepts.summary: Define strength, stiffness, hardness, ductility, toughness and brittleness as distinct properties.

misconceptions.text: Glass is a slow-flowing liquid at room temperature, which is why old windows are thicker at the bottom.
Stiffness and strength mean the same thing.

concepts.name: Hooke's law and elastic modulus
concepts.summary: Apply E to compute elastic deflection or strain under a given load, including Poisson's ratio effects.

concepts.name: Reading stress-strain curves
concepts.summary: Extract Young's modulus, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation and fracture point from a tensile curve.

concepts.name: Point defects and dislocations
concepts.summary: Describe vacancies, interstitials, substitutional atoms and dislocations as imperfections that govern properties.

concepts.name: Slip and plastic deformation in metals
concepts.summary: Explain how dislocation motion on slip systems allows metals to deform plastically at stresses far below the theoretical value.

concepts.name: Grain structure and grain boundaries
concepts.summary: Describe polycrystalline microstructure and how grain boundaries impede dislocation motion.

concepts.name: Reading binary phase diagrams
concepts.summary: Identify phases present and their compositions at a given temperature and apply the lever rule to find phase fractions.

concepts.name: Thermal and electrical property basics
concepts.summary: Relate conductivity, thermal expansion and specific heat to bonding and structure across material classes.

misconceptions.text: Yield strength is the stress at which a material breaks.
Metals are strong because their crystals are perfect.
In a phase diagram, the lever rule gives the composition of the phases rather than their relative amounts.

concepts.name: Strengthening mechanisms in metals
concepts.summary: Apply grain refinement, solid solution, strain hardening and precipitation strengthening to raise strength and predict the ductility trade-off.

concepts.name: Eutectic and eutectoid reactions
concepts.summary: Analyse the iron-carbon diagram to predict equilibrium microstructures such as ferrite, pearlite and cementite.

concepts.name: Diffusion and Arrhenius kinetics
concepts.summary: Use Fick's laws and the temperature dependence of diffusion to estimate rates of processes such as carburising.

concepts.name: Heat treatment of steels
concepts.summary: Use TTT and CCT diagrams to analyse how cooling rate yields pearlite, bainite or martensite and how tempering adjusts properties.

concepts.name: Polymer structure and thermal behaviour
concepts.summary: Relate chain length, crosslinking, crystallinity and the glass transition temperature to polymer stiffness and processing.

concepts.name: Ceramic fracture and flaw statistics
concepts.summary: Analyse why ceramics fail in tension from flaws and why strength varies between nominally identical specimens.

concepts.name: Fracture toughness and stress concentration
concepts.summary: Apply stress concentration factors and fracture toughness to judge whether a cracked component will fracture.

concepts.name: Fatigue and creep failure
concepts.summary: Interpret S-N curves and creep curves to analyse failure under cyclic loads and sustained high-temperature loads.

misconceptions.text: Increasing strength always improves a material's performance, with no cost to ductility or toughness.
Quenched steel is simply harder because it is cooled colder, rather than because of the phase formed.
A component loaded below its yield strength will never fail.

concepts.name: Composite micromechanics
concepts.summary: Predict composite stiffness and strength with iso-strain and iso-stress bounds and analyse the roles of fibre length, orientation and interface.

concepts.name: Property-based material selection
concepts.summary: Derive performance indices for a function, objective and constraints and use property charts to rank candidates.

concepts.name: Viscoelasticity in polymers
concepts.summary: Analyse stress relaxation, creep and temperature dependence of polymer response using viscoelastic models.

concepts.name: Corrosion mechanisms and control
concepts.summary: Analyse electrochemical corrosion types and evaluate protection via coatings, cathodic protection, alloying or design.

concepts.name: Electronic and band properties
concepts.summary: Explain conductor, semiconductor and insulator behaviour via band structure and doping and how temperature and impurities change conductivity.

concepts.name: Fatigue life and damage tolerance
concepts.summary: Evaluate fatigue life using crack growth laws and decide inspection intervals or design changes.

concepts.name: Process-structure-property links
concepts.summary: Evaluate how casting, forming, powder processing and additive manufacturing alter microstructure and resulting properties.

misconceptions.text: The best material is the one with the highest value of a single property such as strength.
Composite properties are simply the average of fibre and matrix properties regardless of loading direction.
Corrosion resistant metals such as stainless steel are immune to corrosion in all environments.

concepts.name: Multi-objective material trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing objectives such as cost, mass, sustainability and risk to justify a material choice under uncertainty.

concepts.name: Hybrid and architected materials
concepts.summary: Design hybrids that fill empty regions of property space by combining materials and geometry.

concepts.name: Microstructure design for target properties
concepts.summary: Specify composition, processing route and heat treatment to produce a microstructure that meets a property set.

concepts.name: Failure analysis and forensics
concepts.summary: Diagnose a service failure from fracture surfaces, microstructure and loading history and judge the root cause.

concepts.name: Life-cycle and sustainability assessment
concepts.summary: Evaluate materials by embodied energy, emissions, recyclability and end-of-life across the product life cycle.

concepts.name: Extreme environment materials
concepts.summary: Design or select materials for extreme temperature, radiation or aggressive chemical conditions, integrating creep, oxidation and degradation.

concepts.name: Computational and data-driven methods
concepts.summary: Evaluate the reliability of modelling and machine learning predictions of properties and decide how to validate them experimentally.

misconceptions.text: Failure analysis can usually identify one single cause, so design and processing need not be considered together.
Recyclable or bio-based materials are always the more sustainable choice.
Computational predictions can replace experimental validation once a model is calibrated.
